Text mining + NLP + machine learning

Can language patterns reveal whether a news story is fake?

An end-to-end fake news detection investigation that combined KNIME data preparation, RapidMiner text mining, TF-IDF and n-gram feature engineering, four classification algorithms, and iterative performance tuning.

Follow the investigationView model resultsView GitHub Repository

Project at a glance

The project began with separate fake and real news files, transformed raw article text into machine-learning features, and compared traditional, ensemble, and neural-network approaches.

01 · Business problem

Misinformation moves faster than manual fact-checking can scale.

Fake news can alter public opinion, weaken trust in journalism, influence elections, and create financial volatility. The project investigated whether linguistic signals could provide a scalable first-pass classification system for identifying suspicious articles before wider distribution.

The analytical question

Can the wording and writing style of an article provide enough evidence for a machine-learning model to distinguish fabricated news from authentic reporting?

Social platforms

Contain rapid spread

Flag suspicious content early enough for review before it reaches a larger audience.

Newsrooms

Support editorial verification

Prioritize articles requiring additional fact-checking without replacing journalists.

Public institutions

Monitor coordinated disinformation

Identify language patterns associated with misleading campaigns and emerging narratives.

03 · KNIME data preparation

I built two parallel data streams and turned them into one labeled corpus.

Fake-news branch

Import, isolate text, and assign class 1

The File Reader loaded fake.csv. A Column Filter kept the article text, and a Constant Value Column assigned the fake-news label.

Real-news branch

Repeat the same logic with class 0

The true.csv file passed through the same sequence so both classes entered the combined dataset with identical structure.

Corpus assembly

Concatenate both streams

The Concatenate node merged the two labeled sources. Missing Value and Duplicate Row Filter nodes then removed incomplete or repeated content that could distort evaluation.

Handoff

Export a clean CSV for text mining

The prepared data was written to CSV so RapidMiner could continue the analysis after KNIME text-processing issues interrupted the original plan.

Report page 5 shows the complete merge, label, missing-value, duplicate-removal, and export process.
04 · Text transformation

Raw articles had to become structured numerical evidence.

The text-processing pipeline standardized language and reduced noise before generating TF-IDF and n-gram features. Each step changed what the models could recognize.

Original text“BREAKING NEWS: The shocking report was released today.”
Lowercase“breaking news: the shocking report was released today.”
Tokenizebreaking · news · the · shocking · report · released · today
Remove stopwordsbreaking · news · shocking · report · released · today
Token filteringRemove punctuation, noise, and low-information tokens.
Stemmingbreaking → break · released → releas
TF-IDFAssign larger weights to terms that distinguish one article from the larger corpus.
N-gramsPreserve phrases such as “breaking news” instead of treating every word independently.
Report page 6 shows the RapidMiner document-processing chain: tokenization, case transformation, stopword filtering, token filtering, stemming, and n-gram generation.
Why TF-IDF mattered

Words appearing in almost every article receive little weight, while terms that are unusually important within a specific article receive greater influence. This helped the models focus on distinguishing vocabulary rather than raw word counts.

06 · Experimentation and tuning

The final performance came from repeated changes, not one model run.

Train-test split experiment

The initial 80/20 approach was changed to 90/10 after Naïve Bayes improved from roughly 83% to 88%. This gave the models more training examples, though future work should confirm the result with cross-validation rather than one split.

Epoch experiment

The neural network began at 10 epochs. Increasing training to 30 epochs raised reported performance to approximately 92%, demonstrating that the model needed additional optimization cycles.

Sample-size experiment

Smaller stratified samples of approximately 500 records reportedly produced stronger accuracy and reduced computational failures. This was practical for limited hardware, but it also limits generalizability.

Tree-model tuning

Gradient Boosted Trees benefited from learning-rate, depth, and iteration tuning. Random Forest remained weak, reinforcing that algorithms effective on structured data may not transfer well to sparse text vectors.

What I would improve in a production study

I would use stratified cross-validation, fixed random seeds, a larger reproducible sample, and a documented hyperparameter search. The reported 92% should be treated as the best project experiment, not yet as a production benchmark.

07 · Performance results

Deep Learning led every reported metric.

92%Accuracy
90%Precision
91%Recall
91%F1 score
Report page 13 compares accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 across all four models.
Why Deep Learning won

The neural network was better able to combine many weak textual signals into nonlinear patterns. Naïve Bayes remained a strong low-cost baseline, while Random Forest struggled with sparse high-dimensional vectors and Gradient Boosted Trees offered a middle ground.

08 · Linguistic findings and business use

The analysis suggested that fabricated stories relied more heavily on emotionally charged language.

The report identified sensational expressions such as “breaking news,” “shocking,” and “unbelievable” as patterns associated with fabricated articles, while authentic news was described as more neutral and factual. These are correlations in the analyzed corpus, not universal proof that an individual story is false.

Social media moderation

Use model scores to prioritize suspicious content for review before it gains wider reach.

Editorial fact-checking

Route articles with unusual linguistic patterns to journalists for additional verification.

Government monitoring

Track emerging disinformation narratives while preserving human and legal oversight.

Financial risk monitoring

Identify potentially misleading business stories that could influence investor behavior or corporate reputation.

09 · Challenges and problem-solving

The project changed direction when the original workflow stopped working.

Tool failure

KNIME text-mining operators produced errors

Even after extensions were checked, required operators were unavailable or unstable. I preserved the working preprocessing portion and moved the modeling stage to RapidMiner.

Hardware limits

High-dimensional text exhausted local resources

The laptop experienced crashes, freezing, and shutdowns when processing larger samples and resource-heavy models.

Workflow redesign

The pipeline became a cross-platform process

Exporting a clean CSV from KNIME created a reliable handoff into RapidMiner, allowing the project to continue without discarding completed work.

Reproducibility

Neural-network results varied across runs

Random initialization produced slight performance changes, highlighting the need for fixed seeds, cross-validation, and documented experiments.

My role

Designed, built, debugged, and interpreted the pipeline

I prepared and labeled the corpus in KNIME, built the RapidMiner text-processing chain, configured and compared four models, tested train-test splits and neural-network epochs, evaluated performance, documented technical challenges, and translated the results into business applications.

Future roadmap

Move from word weighting to contextual language understanding

The next version would use BERT or another transformer model, cloud computing, larger samples, automated tuning, cross-validation, explainability, source metadata, and real-time review workflows.

Project conclusion

The strongest model was only one part of the solution. The real work was transforming messy language into evidence a model could use.

This project demonstrated the full NLP lifecycle: corpus assembly, cleaning, tokenization, stopword removal, stemming, TF-IDF, n-grams, model comparison, tuning, troubleshooting, and business interpretation. It also showed why reported accuracy must be considered alongside sampling, computational constraints, reproducibility, and human verification.
